answer:
At 1 atm, a liquid with 95 mol% ethanol and 5 mol% water is in equilibrium with a vapour of about **94.5 mol% ethanol and 5.5 mol% water**. The bubble point is about **78.2–78.3 °C**.

The vapour has slightly less ethanol than the liquid. That is because 95 mol% is past the ethanol–water azeotrope, so water is the more volatile component at this composition. This is why ordinary distillation cannot get past the azeotrope.

**How I got it:** I calculated the bubble point with modified Raoult's law (ideal gas, activity coefficients in the liquid) using the `thermo` 0.6.1 package. I installed it in a scratch virtual environment and did not change anything in the repository. I used three independent activity-coefficient models:

| Model | T_bubble (°C) | y ethanol | y water | γ ethanol | γ water | Azeotrope it predicts, x ethanol |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| UNIFAC (original) | 78.22 | 0.9449 | 0.0551 | 1.002 | 2.533 | about 0.892 |
| UNIFAC (Dortmund) | 78.30 | 0.9467 | 0.0533 | 1.001 | 2.444 | about 0.894 |
| NRTL (ChemSep parameters) | 78.26 | 0.9455 | 0.0545 | 1.001 | 2.501 | about 0.876 |

The three models agree to within about 0.002 in vapour mole fraction. Each one also predicts an azeotrope at about 88–89 mol% ethanol, which shows they behave correctly near this composition.

**Not checked:** I did not compare against measured VLE data for this exact point. From memory, the literature azeotrope is about 89.4 mol% ethanol at 78.15 °C, which matches the models, but I have not confirmed it against a source.
